The root cap is a specialized structure found at the tip of the root that protects the growing root apex as it pushes through the soil.

It is not found in the shoot system, which typically has buds, leaves, and nodes/internodes.

In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root does not persist. Instead, a fibrous root system develops, where numerous thin roots emerge from the base of the stem. This is different from dicots, where the primary root develops into a taproot system.

Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells in roots that increase the surface area for water and mineral absorption.

They are delicate, single-celled structures that help in efficient nutrient uptake.

Further information:

Trichomes: These are hair-like structures found on stems and leaves, not roots.

Cuticle: A waxy layer present on leaves and stems to prevent water loss, but it is absent in roots to facilitate absorption.

Stomata: Pores present on leaves and stems for gas exchange, not water absorption.

The region of elongation lies just above the meristematic zone. Cells in this region elongate rapidly, contributing to root growth and increasing its length.

Further information:

Region of meristematic activity: This is the area where new cells are produced but not where the root length increases significantly.

Region of maturation: In this region, the cells differentiate into specialized cell types like root hairs, but cell elongation does not occur here.

Root cap: The root cap protects the root tip and aids in soil penetration, but it is not involved in the increase of root length.
The primary function of the stem is support, conduction, and storage, not direct absorption of water and minerals. Absorption is mainly carried out by the root system.

Venation refers to the arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina (leaf blade) of a leaf.

It plays a role in support, transport of nutrients, and photosynthesis.

o Types of venation:

§ Parallel venation (e.g., in monocots like grasses)

§ Reticulate venation (e.g., in dicots like roses and hibiscus)

· Phyllotaxy: Refers to the arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch, not veins in the leaf.

· Aestivation: Refers to the arrangement of flower petals or sepals in a flower bud before it opens.

· Placentation: Refers to the arrangement of ovules within the ovary of a flower.

questions.solution:
Epidermal tissue system → Outermost covering of the plant body

· The epidermal tissue system includes the epidermis, cuticle, and associated structures like stomata and trichomes.

· It serves as a protective layer for the plant, preventing water loss and acting as a barrier against pathogens.

Ground tissue system → Cortex, pith, pericycle

· The ground tissue system consists of parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma cells.

· It is found in areas like the cortex (outer layers of stems and roots), pith (central part of stems), and pericycle (outer boundary of vascular tissues in roots).

· It plays roles in storage, support, and photosynthesis.

Vascular tissue system → Xylem and phloem

· The vascular tissue system includes xylem and phloem, which are responsible for transporting water, minerals, and nutrients throughout the plant.

· Xylem conducts water and minerals from roots to other parts, while phloem transports sugars and other organic nutrients.

· Dicotyledonous plants typically exhibit reticulate venation, where the veins form a network-like pattern (a reticulum) in the leaf.

o This pattern is commonly seen in leaves of plants like roses, bean plants, and oak trees.

Why not the other options?

· Parallel venation: This is characteristic of monocotyledonous plants like grasses, wheat, and lilies.

· Whorled venation: Refers to leaves arranged in a whorl around the stem, not the venation pattern of the leaf itself.

· Alternate venation: Refers to the arrangement of leaves on the stem, not the pattern of veins in the leaf.

· A compound leaf is one where the lamina is divided into multiple leaflets, and the incisions of the leaf reach the midrib, breaking the leaf into several distinct segments.

· Simple leaf is a leaf that has a single, undivided blade.

· Stipulate refers to leaves that have stipules (small leaf-like structures at the base of the petiole), not the division of the leaf into leaflets.

· Sessile refers to leaves that lack a petiole and are directly attached to the stem.

In grasses (monocots), the guard cells of stomata are dumb-bell shaped, unlike the kidney-shaped guard cells found in dicots.

However, vascular bundles in dicot stems are arranged in a ring, not scattered (which is a characteristic of monocots). Therefore, only statement A is correct.

A tissue is a group of similar cells along with intercellular substances that work together to perform a specific function in multicellular organisms.

o Example: Muscle tissue, epithelial tissue, connective tissue, etc.

Further insights:

· Organ: An organ is made up of different types of tissues working together to perform a specific function.

· Organ system: An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform related functions (e.g., the digestive system).

· Cell aggregate: This is not a standard biological term, though it may describe a collection of cells. The correct term for a functional group of similar cells is tissue.

The Indian bullfrog (Rana tigrina), now classified as Hoplobatrachus tigerinus, is the most common frog species in India.

It is large, with a distinctive green and brown coloration, and is commonly found in ponds, marshes, and other water bodies across India.

· Frogs are poikilothermic (cold-blooded), meaning their body temperature fluctuates based on the surrounding environment.

· The nictitating membrane is a transparent third eyelid that protects the frog's eyes underwater while maintaining visibility.

· Frogs are carnivorous, feeding on insects and small animals. Carnivores have a shorter digestive tract because protein-rich food is easier to digest compared to plant material.

· In the epipetalous condition, the stamens are attached to the petals of the flower. This means the stamens are fused with the petals, typically at the base.

o This is commonly seen in plants like Solanum and Nicotiana.

Further information:

· Calyx: The calyx is the outermost whorl of a flower and consists of sepals. The stamens are not attached to the calyx in an epipetalous condition.

· Perianth: The perianth is the combined term for both the calyx (sepals) and corolla (petals). Stamens are not attached to the perianth in this case.

· Gynoecium: The gynoecium refers to the female reproductive parts (carpels), and stamens are typically not attached to the gynoecium in the epipetalous condition.

· Katherine Esau was born in Ukraine in 1898. She studied agriculture in Russia and Germany and received her doctorate in 1931 in United States.

· She reported in her early publications that the curly top virus spreads through a plant via the foodconducting or phloem tissue.

· Dr Esau's Plant Anatomy published in 1954 took a dynamic, developmental approach designed to enhance one's understanding of plant structure and an enormous impact worldwide, literally bringing about a revival of the discipline.

· The Anatomy of Seed Plants by Katherine Esau was published in 1960. It was referred to as Webster's of plant biology - it is encyclopediac.

· In 1957 she was elected to the National Academy of Sciences, becoming the sixth woman to receive that honour.

· In addition to this prestigious award, she received the National Medal of Science from President George Bush in 1989.

· When Katherine Esau died in the year 1997, Peter Raven, director of Anatomy and Morphology, Missouri Botanical Garden, remembered that she 'absolutely dominated' the field of plant biology even at the age of 99.

questions.solution:
Types of Placentation

· Marginal: The ovules develop in rows near the margin on the placenta formed along the ventral suture. It occurs in monocarpellary and unilocular ovary, e.g., Leguminosae.

· Parietal: The placenta is formed by the swelling up of cohering margins, and on the latter develop the ovules in rows. It occurs in bicarpellary or multicarpellary but unilocular ovary, e.g., Papaveraceae. .

· Axile: Here, the placentae develop from the central axis which correspond to the confluent margins of carpels. It occurs in bi-to multilocular ovary, e.g., Solanaceae, Malvaceae.

· Free-central: Here, the placenta develop in the centre of the ovary as a prolongation of floral axis and the ovules are attached on this axis. It occurs in multicarpellary but unilocular ovary, e.g., Primulaceae

· Basal: The placenta develops directly on the thalamus and bears a single ovule at the base of the unilocular ovary, e.g., Compositae.

· In isobilateral leaves (found in monocots like grasses), stomata are present on both upper and lower surfaces, and the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers.

· Along the veins in these leaves, certain adaxial epidermal cells modify into large, empty, colourless cells called bulliform cells.

· Function of bulliform cells:

o When they are turgid (full of water), the leaf remains open for photosynthesis.

o When they are flaccid (due to water loss), the leaf curls inward to reduce water loss.

This adaptation helps monocot plants conserve water under dry conditions.

· The vertical section of a dorsiventral leaf through the lamina shows three main

parts, namely, epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system.

· The epidermis which covers both the upper surface (adaxial epidermis) and lower surface (abaxial epidermis) of the leaf has a conspicuous cuticle.

· The abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata than the adaxial

epidermis. The latter may even lack stomata.

· The tissue between the upper and the lower epidermis is called the mesophyll.

· Mesophyll, which possesses chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis, is made up of parenchyma.

· It has two types of cells - the palisade parenchyma and the spongy parenchyma.

· The adaxially placed palisade parenchyma is made up of elongated cells, which are arranged vertically and parallel to each other.

· The oval or round and loosely arranged spongy parenchyma is situated below the palisade cells and extends to the lower epidermis.

· There are numerous large spaces and air cavities between these cells.

· The correct term for the parenchymatous cells between the xylem and phloem is the conjunctive tissue.

· Stele refers to the central vascular cylinder that includes pericycle, vascular tissues (xylem & phloem), and pith.

Outermost layer - Epiblema

· The epiblema (also called rhizodermis) is the outermost layer of the dicot root.

· It helps in water absorption and often bears root hairs.

Innermost layer of cortex - Endodermis

· The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex.

· It has Casparian strips, which control the movement of water and solutes into the vascular tissue.

Thick-walled parenchymatous cells - Pericycle

· The pericycle is a single layer of thin-walled or thick-walled parenchyma cells just inside the endodermis.

· It gives rise to lateral roots, vascular cambium, and cork cambium.

The floral diagram and floral formula in Figure represents the mustard plant (Family: Brassicaceae).

· The floral formula is represented by some symbols. In the floral formula, Br stands for bracteate, K stands for calyx , C for corolla, P for perianth, A for androecium and G for Gynoecium, Ḡ for superior ovary and G(with underline under G) for inferior ovary, ♂ for male, ♀ for female, ⚤ for bisexual plants, ⊕ for actinomorphic and % for zygomorphic nature of flower. Fusion is indicated by enclosing the figure within bracket and adhesion by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts.

· A floral diagram provides information about the number of parts of a flower, their arrangement and the relation they have with one another (In Figure ). The position of the mother axis with respect to the flower is represented by a dot on the top of the floral diagram. Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium are drawn in successive whorls, calyx being the outermost and the gynoecium being in the centre. Floral formula also shows cohesion and adhesion within parts of whorls and between whorls.
